When we were teenagers, I never saw him as good-looking or talented or anything. He was just an out of control teenager. I almost got into a fight with him at one stage.

All the missteps he made in his career were from trying to do Hollywood blockbuster roles. All the successes were from doing quirky, more artistic films.

## 2. Pandorum (2009). What a good sci-fi horror movie.

**Score:** 374
**Body:**   
I love sci-fi movies in general, especially those about people trapped on a spaceship traveling through deep space for years. I adore \*Passengers\*, for instance. 

I recently stumbled upon \*Pandorum\* while looking through lists of forgotten sci-fi films. I didn't expect it to be so fast-paced and exciting. I don't care that it was a box-office flop or low-budget; it kept me on the edge of my seat the whole time, and the plot twists felt well-earned. 

The film also features a surprisingly large number of familiar faces. Besides Dennis Quaid and Ben Foster, Norman Reedus makes an unexpected appearance. 

There’s Antje Traue—the actress who played Zod’s tough lieutenant (Faora-Ul) in \*Man of Steel\*—and Cam Gigandet, who played the villain in the first \*Twilight\* movie. It’s a shame his career didn't really take off; he’s an interesting actor. 

The story follows two crew members who wake up on a colony ship traveling to a distant planet; they can't figure out why they weren't woken up during their scheduled shift, and the door is sealed shut.

## 4. Ken Russell's The Devils is as wild today as it was 60 years ago

**Score:** 123
**Body:** I saw The Devils for the first time in 2000 on a battered VHS tape, re-recorded at least five times over, in edited form, butchered by pearl-clutching censors from another country. It wasn't ideal in any way, yet even then, it left an inescapable impression. I didn't understand most of it; I was 14 - how could I? But I understood the feeling it left behind.

Another 25 years later, The Devils finally returns in its completed form, proving itself a sublime, timeless provocation that has lost none of its potency. Meticulously restored, the 4K print looks as if it was shot yesterday. I know I watched The Devils in my youth, but I did not truly see it until now.

Set in Loudon during the seventeenth century, The Devils is a loosely historical retelling of the witch trial and execution of Father Grandier (Oliver Reed), who is accused of satanic acts involving a local convent comprised entirely of women. Their leader, Sister Jeanne (Vanessa Redgrave), lusts after Grandier and watches him hungrily through the bars of their reclusive home. When the lecherous priest marries, her desperation sparks a lie that gives the Catholic church the excuse they need to tear down Grandier's haven.

Naturally, the church cares little for what Grandier does to his flock. They're more interested in the power of the self-governing Loudon and the ensuing war between Protestants and Catholics vying for the seat of power in France. Russell's distaste for those in power doesn't pick sides; everyone is a hypocrite, some just have fancier robes.

The story itself is simple; everything around it is not. This is a moody, ostentatious melodrama, intentionally operatic and grandiose to make sense of the world. In its opening scene, we witness Grandier abandon his latest mistress when she announces her pregnancy. He declares himself ready to die, if only someone would grant him that peace. 

Around them, Loudon's streets fill with the dead and dying from the plague. It's as if the world is ending, or it always was, and we weren't paying attention.

As the church descends on Loudon, they're joined by a witch-hunter (Michael Gothard) who claims he can spot the devil's influence through "science". Naturally, said science is merely torture, including forced enemas and beatings, and all of it is an excuse to exert power over those who can't defend themselves. In one of the most horrifying sequences, Russell brilliantly pulls the rug from under our feet, shifting the mood from acerbic farce to gruesome horror within seconds as Loudon's sanctity is broken.

It's here The Devil's proves most fascinating. Beyond its blustering and humorous satire, Russell's brilliantly composed film is really about the different aspects of systemic power and its abuses. Grandier calls himself a man of god, yet fucks anything with a pulse and a smile. Jeanne leads her Ursuline convent in moral seclusion, yet dreams of wild sexual acts with a man she doesn't know. The churches themselves are merely ornate bureaucracies more concerned with amassing power than deliverance.

Throughout the decades, The Devils has garnered a reputation as a blasphemous, morally putrid film. Today, that reputation feels almost quaint. You can find worse imagery on Instagram. But the symbolism has lost none of its power.

Derek Jarman's striking set design and Shirley Russell's lush costuming evoke the romanticism of grand BBC dramas, which The Devil's proudly tears down with gleeful abandon. Watch, for example, how Grandier swoops up and down Loudon's streets like a perpetually erect Don Giovanni, and tell me that's not Russell cackling at the empty meaning we attach to manmade objects. A cross is a cross, Russell suggests; using it for masturbation is no less an affront than crucifixion.

It's coming out on October 16th, and it's totally worth seeing in cinemas. 

Full review here:  

https://regionfree.net/ken-russells-the-devils-4k-restoration-review/

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Digger's box office performance as metatextual commentary

**Score:** 21
**Body:** Spoilers obviously


One of the central messages of Digger is highlighted in the confrontation between the director and Tom Cruise's character near the end of the film. 


Tom Cruise argues that this farcical performance lacks truth, is in poor taste, etc. The director on the other hand makes the case that satire is important, even of cruel events; people need to be able to laugh at it, otherwise the reality is just too depressing.


Now it is not entirely clear which side of the argument the film agrees with - not that it even has to necessarily - but for me it seems like the film is making the case for the director's side of things. Especially with the final scene of the crowd responding to the performance with enthusiastic applause.



However, coming to reality and looking at things from a more meta level. The Digger trailer shows that it is some sort of absurd political satire. The Trump parody aspect was not super clear in the trailer, but it has something to do with climate change, something akin to Don't Look Up. People saw this trailer starring Tom Cruise, a A-Lister, and chose **not** to go see it. 



Perhaps people aren't in the mood to laugh at the people and systems ruining the planet, driving us towards armageddon. Similar thing happened with "The Apprentice": a great film, but underseen and underappreciated. Primarily, I think, because it was an unflattering biopic about Donald Trump which means a) fans of his don't want to see him criticized and b) people who hate him didn't want to voluntarily be subjected to more Trump content.



Anyways, I personally like “Digger” on a conceptual/intellectual level though moment-to-moment when watching the over-the-top satire scenes, I was emotionally quite disconnected. Felt more in synch with the Cruise character than the director. 



I would've preferred it wasn't a flop. But it is interesting how the film's box office performance plays into (one of) the central themes of the film itself.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I don’t think the film agrees with Cruise’s character or the director. I think it agrees with the producer who says ‘it doesn’t matter.’ The point is that political art that critiques the elite is something made by the elite and that those making it benefit financially and personally (the daughter subplot) from their association with them.

Meanwhile the art itself provides, at best, some momentary catharsis that changes nothing (they all still exit out into a broken world). At worst, it is a distraction that allows those in power to keep doing what they’re doing (“Panic is a resource. When the house is burning down, no one cares who left the toaster on.”).

The final sound cue basically asks the audience what the hell they’re doing there. The advertising brought people in to see broad political satire but the film clearly believes that doing so is a waste of time. It’s basically goading the viewer to go out and do something other than just passively watch a movie.
  - yours is the first review where i feel like the message of the film finally got through. 

OP says that the final scene of the crowd applauding suggests that the film supports the director’s pro-satire sentiment. but that is not the final scene in the film. 
  - I do think that last paragraph is a big part of why people are annoyed at the movie. If you’re going to tell us that passively watching a movie is a waste of time and not meaningful action (fair enough so far), and you want us to go out and do something, I think your movie better have some ideas for things you might want us to go out and do. If we take Tom Cruise’s monologue at face value instead of just the villain of the story deflecting, the answer is “stop using TikTok and flying to Mallorca” I guess? At every turn the climate apocalypse is presented as something too big for individual action to matter (even the president’s individual actions don’t matter, nature is too far gone and either we get lucky with its course or we don’t), and from where I’m sitting that’s also true of the real world we live in. So the movie is full of things it tells us NOT to do, but I don’t hear one good suggestion for what we should do. 

And if we want to get meta about this, if passively watching a movie satirizing rich people and politicians destroying the environment is unproductive and wasteful, then the people who made the movie were being equally unproductive and wasteful. If Iñárritu wants change in the world, then he should be picketing in the streets or trying to launch a coup I guess, because making a satirical movie is pointless. Surely Tom Cruise, who I presume flew private when he was making the movie instead of using his hundreds of millions of dollars on polar bear sanctuaries, is far more implicated by the film than I was for buying a ticket. 

I’m not even negative on Digger as a film, I think it works more than it doesn’t, but you can only be so smug about telling the audience they’re doing something wrong before the audience, justifiably, turns the mirror around on you.  
    - I think you’re taking the societal critique too literally. I don’t think Iñárritu is criticising the audience as much as he is an artist making art about making art under fascism. The cherry on top of the irony cake is this film coming out by WB the same week that the Donald Trump approved Paramount merger went through. It definitely is skeptical of satire, but it clearly is an auteur exorcising his frustrations at the world, not a lecture about why you’re bad for watching it or using TikTok.  
2. I think a major problem with satire in general over the last decade or so is that satire works best in "emperor has no clothes" situations. As in, something has fairly obvious flaws but the dominant public sentiment is that it's perfect. Satire might be the only way to even approach the subject when there is heavy censorship of overtly political criticism. But even when there is no actual barrier to direct criticism, satire can help create enough distance from the actual issue to force people to examine it from a different viewpoint.

Modern social media has made it nearly impossible for this kind of situation to happen. Negative takes on nearly anything have become mainstream, to the point where any extremely popular artist, athlete, or actor will be heavily criticized for any perceived flaw. The scandals and controversies around celebrities get more press and reach than the actual things they are famous for.

If Digger is meant to be a meta-commentary on other satires like Don't Look Up, it's hurt by the fact that Don't Look Up itself was widely criticized directly when it was released for roughly the same reasons. If public sentiment is already negative, the same satire that would be considered clever and insightful might just be seen as mean-spirited and piling on.
3. I think it’s p firmly against satire as a tool. Fossil Fools is a moronic play that simplifies the narrative and acts as propaganda. Digger Rockwell becomes an eccentric whose worst traits are irrational bumbling, not the cold hard reality of his indifference to suffering and the neoliberal systems that enabled his existence. His nephew is fucking funding it lol, and in the process laundering his reputation as a false act of penance. The bourgeois audience cheers and then has to go outside into the absolute hell they have facilitated by paying for this crap, safely rationalising their complicity by pretending that entertaining themselves is action. Digger (the movie) seems to be disgusted by the notion that art can change anything, and tbh it’s right. 
  - I also think it’s worth noting Plemons owns a surveillance company and then we go outside to see a world with armed robot police and drones circling 
4. I don't think that was Trump. Do you see Trump praying and having a Bible advisor following him around, that he would take seriously? It's likely a mix, closer to Reagan, then Trump. But it's George Bush, it's Biden, it's Trump, it's Clinton it's a character of an American president. 

Also, Tom is having a hard time making this play satirical, when his daughter is missing due to the events that are still unfolding 25 years later. When the play is trying to bring closure to something that hasn't ended and is still affecting his real life in real time. 
  - I mean President Goodman also at the end insulted the Bible and kicked out the reverend on his ass. Very Trumpian lol. But agree that the president is less supposed to be a pure Trump stand-in than a mutated fusion of American presidents
  - >Do you see Trump praying and having a Bible advisor following him around, that he would take seriously?

Yes. Does this look familiar, maybe an identical visual in Digger?

He may not take them seriously, but still. This happened in real life and that's why it's in the movie.

It isn't a one-on-one and there for sure are parallels to other US Presidents and the institution as a whole, but it is also obviously a Trump parody/homage.

## 2. The final argument scene Digger and the purpose of art

**Score:** 14
**Body:** So, after seeing Digger, I ended up liking it more than I disliked it and honestly I kind of like it a bit more after ruminating on it a bit more. But I just want to put my thoughts into words on the argument scene towards the end that occurs between Rockwell, Hannah, and Kenny. Spoilers obviously.

To those who either don’t remember or haven’t seen it and will probably not see it (which seems to be the case for most lol), the argument starts with Tom Cruise’s character finally having enough of his portrayal of Digger Rockwell and complains to Hannah, the director, saying that the exaggerated version is not true to who Digger was that brings down the whole play. After some back and forth, Hannah keeps pointing to the fact that his portrayal is supposed to be funny and that the play is a satire that is meant as a condemnation of not just Digger but everyone of his generation that created the hellscape they currently live in.

Kenny, Digger’s nephew, interjects, saying that they are both right and that the main purpose of the play was that the audience needs to laugh at it, a way to relieve themselves of the tragedy that actually occurred. Please keep in mind this is a just a plain summary that doesn’t fully capture what was said in the argument.

I keep thinking about this scene because I believe each character represents a different purpose that art is supposed to serve. For Tom Cruise’s character, his camp is art as truth. As an actor, his main goal is to properly portray who Digger actually was and to encompass him as accurately as possible, as anything less would be a failure in his eyes and to the play as a whole. He’s sees this exaggerated version of Digger as an insult to art because it fails to show truth. Hannah counters this with her camp, art as power. She if fully in on the play as a satire and its purpose going far beyond showing what actually happened. She sees the exaggeration as a statement to be made to those in power, portraying them in this way as a takedown of the people that destroyed their world and those that continue to do it.

Kenny’s position is interesting because it’s still very similar to Hannah’s camp but I believe he encompasses art as entertainment. He does believe that there needs to be a condemnation of Digger, but not as a message for those in power but as an outlet for the audience’s grievances. Simply, turning the tragedy into a comedy just so the audience can feel good for a short while. This position is interesting coming from him because I see normal people have this position as well when it comes to the art they interact with, i.e., they just want escape their lives for a short time and have fun, but, in this case, this idea is coming from Digger’s nephew who’s producing the play. ## 4. Bullitt (1968)

Rating: 9.5/10

Watched: October 2, 2026



I have to confess, I was expecting a very different movie from the one I watched, and I'm not mad about it. Part of my preconceptions about Bullitt has a lot to do with the fact that the only thing I KNEW about this movie was about it's legendary car chase scene.



I promised myself I 'wasn't gonna be the guy' who talked about the car chase scene because everyone always talks about the car chase scene but you know what?



It absolutely deserves it. The clip I included was because of the specific shot of the bad guys seeing Bullitt's famous car appearing behind them in the rearview mirror. The slickness of that moment absolutely sold the scene to me in an instant. It was so very well done, and the resulting chase through the incredibly steep hills of San Francisco, sometimes narrowly missing a full-on crash, all the way out of the city is some of the most tense car driving I think I've ever seen. My stomach rose and fell as those rad old muscle cars went flying up and down those hills and you just have to give kudos to the drivers and the camera people because for some of the hairier shots, they were IN the damn cars. 



So, going in knowing only that it has an exceptional chase scene led me to believe I was in for a kind of proto-Dirty Harry-esque kind of affair with plenty of violence, and that was a thing I was fully ready to accept.



But what I got was something I love even more than that: a rock solid police procedural with a bona fide mystery at the core and plenty of thoughtful, considerate work to solve the case. And what a case it is. 



From the moment things started developing, I was certain I knew who was involved, why Bullitt's case was going sideways and how people were always seemingly one step ahead of him. I'm sure the director wanted us to think that and it worked like a charm, because it sure seemed like Bullitt was thinking along the same lines. 



I can't say anything more than that about the movie's actual plot because to do so might affect your ability to enjoy it, so I'll leave this in closing; 



Lt. Frank Bullitt's investigation into the murder of a gangster turning State's evidence and the attempted murder of police officers results in more than one exhilarating chase, a few shootouts, and the use of genuine police protocol to catch the real bad guy.



And that? That's a great combination!
